summary: This paper proposes a stacked-annulus architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing that organizes data tiles in concentric rings around a central compute region, jointly optimizing execution latency and data-tile density. The design includes workload-aware qubit placement based on T-gate and Y-gate characteristics, a selective fast-Y optimization knob, and support for concurrent multi-workload execution.
motivation: Existing FTQC surface-code architectures optimize either execution time (sacrificing data-tile density) or qubit density (sacrificing latency), and they neglect workload-specific characteristics and concurrent execution scenarios. This creates a coupling between space and time costs that prior work treats independently.
method: The authors propose placing data patches in stacked annular rings around a central compute region and develop a directed annular movement (DAM) strategy with bounded radial and angular displacement. They introduce a workload-aware placement algorithm that scores qubits by their T-load, Y-load, and multi-qubit interaction degree, then greedily assigns highest-cost qubits to innermost rings. A selective fast-Y optimization upgrades qubits to two-tile encoding only when measurement speedup ($5t \to 1t$) exceeds the movement penalty. Multi-workload execution uses per-workload quota allocation via computed budgets $B_0(w)$ and $B_Y(w)$.
result: On near-term FTQC benchmarks (quantum chemistry, arithmetic circuits, QFT), the architecture maintains near-optimal cycles-per-T-instruction while using $\sim 21\%$ fewer data tiles than prior dense designs and $\sim 9.3$–$43.4\%$ fewer tiles than the fast-block design. The fast-Y knob delivers $\sim 2.42 \times$ measurement speedup and $\sim 10.86\%$ CPI$_T$ reduction. Under 10-way concurrency, the sharing policy achieves $\sim 90\%$ efficiency with mean slowdown $\sim 1.1 \times$.
